sourceInformation.source: Brigandine: The Legend of Forsena (Hearty Robin, PlayStation, 1998). Only the title is a nod; the world, cast, art and music are original.
sourceInformation.genre: Turn-based grand strategy with a tactical RPG hex-battle layer
sourceInformation.perspective: Campaign: a three-quarter diorama of the continent, north up. Battles: a tilted overhead hex board with billboard figures (tilt toggle). Story: side-on stage scenes with live portraits.
sourceInformation.tech: my-3D2dge 0.85.2 (single-file engine, unmodified) with plain JavaScript; AI Hub Session Protocol v1 client 1.4.0; Playwright 1.63 and Node 24 for tests only. No other libraries.
sourceInformation.artDirection: The engine's native HD-rig style: Humanoid knights with live portraits, six hand-built creature bodies drawn from pixel primitives, season palettes, drawn hexes, a clock-face continent.
sourceInformation.animation: The engine's Humanoid rig and E.Attack moves, plus new creature animation (hops, wing-flaps, squash, lunges), season effects (wildfire, ice, gale motes) and spell bursts.
sourceInformation.audio: All in code: ten step-sequenced songs, about thirty sound effects and Animalese babble voices pitched per speaker, through the engine's synthesiser.
sourceInformation.online: AI Hub shared-world mode (2-4 players): the host's copy orders every command, all copies replay the same seeded battle; seats one and two duel and others watch. Passes the hub harness at 2, 3 and 4 players (latency, loss), host-leave and no-player-host scenarios. Local hot-seat: a campaign for 2-4 humans on one machine (pass-and-play) and a two-human skirmish.
sourceInformation.testing: Headless scripts only (node tests/run.mjs: 522 checks incl. a scripted whole-campaign playthrough), a balance bot, browser screenshots for looks, and the AI Hub harness.
sourceInformation.research: Light: read the plan, the engine card and the hub protocol; no outside research.
sourceInformation.environment: Claude Code CLI (headless); Linux; browser unknown (Chromium via Playwright used for checks)

testingFeedback: Nine: Meridian was one road away from the player's start, so a scripted playthrough won on turn 1; the campaign scene read its map rectangle and cursor before the first draw (crash headless and on loading a save); the first story event fired on turn 1 by mistake; deep links were overwritten by the engine's boot; the attract mode exited itself in a test because of its own activity stamp; the font cannot draw several symbols I had used (shown as ?); and the engine's corner buttons covered my HUD.
Three: the Meridian shortcut (the demo could be finished in one season) and the two first-draw crashes in the campaign scene.
The scripted whole-campaign playthrough plus the all-AI balance bot: they drove every system from the title to an ending in seconds and exposed the Meridian shortcut that no unit test would have.
The data-validation suite (castles, maps, skills, roads, walkable maps in all four seasons): it never failed once, so it protects the future more than it informed the present.
engineFeedback: game.advance with game.debug: the same inputs give the same game, so I could play the whole demo in Node. The Humanoid rigs with live portraits also looked good with no art work, and pause, settings, saves and per-device button labels came free.

Yes. I assumed the font had the pad symbols that input.label returns (a cross, circle, square, triangle) and common punctuation; it does not, so I drew the symbols by hand. A game.go() made before boot finishes is silently replaced by the first scene, and game.every timers vanish at each scene change.

The hex board and its picking, six creature painters, a 10-foot UI kit (focus model, lists, prompts, sliders, talk box), the battle and campaign simulations with their AIs, and the Animalese voices and songs.

Fitting a strategy game to an engine whose views assume a world with a ground plane: I drew everything through r.overlay and did my own depth ordering and picking. The API index is also very large to search for a name.
Ship a small 10-foot UI toolkit (pad and mouse focus, lists, grids, glyph prompts) and a font that includes controller glyphs and common symbols.
promptFeedback: The task's spec for controller-first play, attract mode and dev mode was concrete, and the plan's exact rules and tables made the design decisions quick.

The plan was written for another model, effort and date and names a different file and folder than TASK.md, and its scope (25 castles, 36 knights, 30 species, 13 maps, 40 events) is far beyond one session. TASK.md wins, but I had to reconcile them.

Writing the plan's full content (25 castles, 36 knights, 30 species with 3 forms, 13 maps, 40 events) in one session, and keeping a hex battle readable at 320x240. Shipping all of the plan's tables (100 skills incl. tier and season variants and monster traits, 33 items, 23 classes) and 2-4 side skirmishes took a generalised battle simulation.
Mark which parts of the plan are optional and give a size budget, make the plan's file names agree with TASK.md, and say whether the About screen, chat reply and JSON must match word for word.

aiHub.name: Brigantime: The Legend of Forseasons
aiHub.description: Four season-realms race to Meridian before the Hour-Candle burns out: muster knights and monsters, march on castles, and fight hex battles where the season changes the field. Play a whole campaign, a skirmish, or the same seeded battle against friends in an AI Hub round.
aiHub.controls: D-pad/stick or arrows/WASD move, Cross/Enter confirm, Circle/Backspace back, Square/Space commands or end phase, Triangle/Tab details, mouse hover and click
